questions: How many unit cubes fill the shape, and how do you know?
What does volume tell us about a shape?
segments.say: Volume as unit-cube counting. Show the cubes arriving one at a time and count aloud to 6: the volume is 6 unit cubes. Keep your student notes open at the volume and unit cube definitions for this scene.

questions: How many cubes are in one layer, and how did you work it out?
What is 4 × 3 × 2, and what does each number stand for?
segments.say: Cuboid volume = length × width × height. Count one layer, 4 × 3 = 12 cubes, then stack the second layer for 24 unit cubes. Now try the cuboid questions on the worksheet in pairs.

questions: How many millilitres are there in 1 L?
Would you measure a small cup in millilitres or litres, and why?
segments.say: Liquid volume: millilitres and litres. Watch the small cup fill to 500 mL and the big jug fill to 1 L, and stress the conversion 1 L = 1000 mL: millilitres for small amounts, litres for big ones.

questions: The tall stack looks bigger - does it hold more?
How does counting the cubes settle the question?
segments.say: Watch out: a taller container holds more - or does it? Show the 6 cubes in a tall stack, then rearranged wide: it is the same 6 cubes. Finish by taking the exit ticket on your own - its first question revisits exactly this trap.
segments.watchFor: The taller container holds more. Listen and look for it in pair talk and on the worksheet: Height dominates the eye, so taller looks like more. Send them back to scene s4 and to the correct turn: Count the unit cubes: six cubes is six cubes; shape never changes the amount.
